claim: A meta-analysis can be part of a systematic review, but a systematic review can exist without one; they are not synonyms.
limitations: Abstract does not state the distinction verbatim; the distinction is standard (Cochrane Handbook ch.1) but the Handbook was not read this session.

claim: Scoping reviews are appropriate to identify knowledge gaps, scope a body of literature, clarify concepts or investigate research conduct, and may precede a systematic review.
limitations: Single group's (JBI) guidance; other groups' views on scope/appraisal differ.

claim: PRISMA-ScR is the reporting guideline for scoping reviews (20 essential items + 2 optional).
limitations: Check for newer scoping-review reporting updates before use.

claim: SWiM is a reporting guideline for synthesis without meta-analysis of effect estimates in reviews of interventions (nine items).
limitations: Scope limited to intervention reviews with quantitative data.

claim: In a pilot randomised study of 31 clinicians, PICO-based search templates showed a higher-precision trend but no statistically significant difference versus standard PubMed searching.
limitations: Small pilot; evaluates search interfaces, not question quality.

claim: I-squared depends on study precision and can approach 100% as studies get larger even when tau-squared is unchanged; tau-squared rather than I-squared should guide judgments of clinical relevance of heterogeneity.
limitations: Argument concerns using I2 to decide on pooling; does not say I2 is useless.

claim: H and I-squared (Q-based) are proposed as measures of heterogeneity impact independent of the number of studies and the effect metric, to be reported in preference to the Q test.
limitations: Later literature (Rucker 2008) cautions about I2's dependence on precision.

claim: Fixed-effect and random-effects models embody different assumptions and are not interchangeable; model choice should reflect the goals/context of the analysis.
limitations: Tutorial/position paper by authors of a widely used textbook; other methodologists hold different defaults.

claim: Langan et al. (2019) recommended REML for estimating the heterogeneity variance, found DerSimonian-Laird negatively biased with small studies and rare binary outcomes, and Paule-Mandel positively biased with large differences in study size; they caution tau-squared is unreliable with few studies.
limitations: Simulation scenarios are finite; the recommendation is conditional on them. MetaLab therefore presents REML as a reasonable default, not as universally optimal.

claim: Veroniki et al. (2016) found Paule-Mandel generally, and REML for continuous data, better alternatives to DerSimonian-Laird; Q-profile is recommended for tau-squared confidence intervals.
limitations: Qualitative evaluation + expert consensus, as the abstract itself states.

claim: The Hartung-Knapp(-Sidik-Jonkman) approach keeps nominal coverage better than usual fixed/random-effects tests in simulations and is robust to the tau-squared estimator.
limitations: Hartung & Knapp 2001 studied binary outcomes; the robustness-to-estimator statement comes from Langan 2019 (C009). Truncation (q*<1) handling varies between software.

claim: A prediction interval describes the range of true effects in a new study and should accompany random-effects results.
limitations: Bibliographic record verified (title: 'Interpretation of random effects meta-analyses') but content NOT examined; claim rests on standard methodological practice.

claim: The t(k-2) prediction interval for k>=3 studies (Riley 2011) differs from metafor's default z-based interval; both are implemented and benchmarked.
limitations: The t(k-2) formula itself is checked only against our own computation of it, not against an independent implementation.

claim: The exact small-sample correction J = Gamma(df/2)/(sqrt(df/2)Gamma((df-1)/2)) differs by ~1% from 1-3/(4df-1) at df=2.
limitations: Original paper not read; exact form confirmed by metafor agreement to 1e-9.

claim: Several lifespan-intervention meta-analyses already exist (e.g., DR in rodents, rapamycin in mice, rapamycin vs metformin in vertebrates), so DR/rapamycin lifespan is a crowded area.
limitations: One database; reviews' scope/overlap not read; this is a signal, not a novelty determination.
